title: Spione
byline: Silent spy thriller by Fritz Lang (Fritz Lang-Film GmbH / UFA, Germany, 1928); original screenplay by Lang and Thea von Harbou.

evidence.note: Published 1928. US copyright for pre-1978 works has a maximum term of 95 years from publication (28-year initial term plus up to 67-year renewal term under the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act). A 1928 publication's copyright expired January 1, 2024. As of September 2026 the print is in the US public domain by term.
evidence.source: US Copyright Office â€” How Long Does Copyright Protection Last?

evidence.note: Spione is a German production (Fritz Lang-Film GmbH, distributed by UFA) and not a US work. Under the URAA (1994), foreign works that entered US public domain due to failure of formalities could have copyright restored if still protected in their source country on January 1, 1996. Fritz Lang died August 2, 1976; Germany's life-plus-70-years term therefore runs until 2046, so the film was protected in Germany on the URAA reference date and restoration could have applied. However, URAA restoration cannot extend a work's US term beyond the statutory maximum. For a 1928 publication the ceiling is 95 years from first publication, expiring January 1, 2024. The print is in the US public domain regardless of whether URAA restoration ever applied.
evidence.source: Duke Law Center for the Study of the Public Domain â€” Public Domain Day 2024

evidence.note: Spione is a silent film and carried no original recorded soundtrack. All commercially circulating versions are accompanied by modern commissioned scores: Neil Brand composed the score on the Kino Lorber Blu-ray release; Donald Sosin composed the score on the Kino Lorber DVD release. Both are independently copyrighted compositions and sound recordings tied to the 2004 Murnau Stiftung restoration. The underlying 1928 imagery is in the public domain; any modern musical accompaniment attached to a specific print is separately protected.
evidence.source: Kino Lorber â€” Spies (Restored Authorized Edition)

evidence.note: The screenplay is an original work written in 1928 by Fritz Lang and Thea von Harbou for the film â€” it was not adapted from any prior published work. Thea von Harbou's novel of the same title appeared in 1929, after the film's release, making it a novelization rather than a source text. As an original 1928 work, the screenplay's US copyright expired January 1, 2024 (1928 + 95-year maximum term).
evidence.source: US Copyright Office â€” How Long Does Copyright Protection Last?

evidence.note: The Friedrich-Wilhelm-Murnau-Stiftung completed a 2004 digital restoration of Spione, sourced from surviving nitrate prints â€” the original negative no longer exists. The restored version is distributed on Blu-ray and DVD by Kino Lorber in the US (Blu-ray score: Neil Brand; DVD score: Donald Sosin) and on Blu-ray by Eureka Video (Masters of Cinema) in the UK. As a newly assembled, color-graded, digitally cleaned compilation of archival materials, the restoration constitutes a separately copyrightable work. The commissioned scores on each edition are additionally protected as independent compositions and sound recordings.

editorial:
Spione â€” released in the United States as Spies â€” is a 1928 German silent espionage thriller directed by Fritz Lang, the first film produced by his own company, Fritz Lang-Film GmbH, and distributed by UFA. Rudolf Klein-Rogge plays Haghi, a wheelchair-using banking magnate who secretly commands a global spy network; Willy Fritsch plays the German counter-intelligence agent sent to stop him. The film is regularly cited as a foundational prototype of the spy genre, establishing conventions â€” the criminal mastermind hiding behind a legitimate public identity, double agents, the ticking-clock finale â€” that would recur across decades of successors. The screenplay was an original work by Lang and his then-wife Thea von Harbou; her novel of the same name appeared in 1929 only after the film was already in release, making it a novelization rather than a source text.

The 1928 print and the original story are both in the US public domain by term â€” the maximum 95-year copyright for a 1928 publication expired January 1, 2024. Spione is a German production and could in principle have been subject to URAA restoration (Fritz Lang died in 1976, so German protection runs until 2046, and the film was still protected there on the 1996 URAA reference date), but URAA restoration cannot push a 1928 work's US term past its 95-year ceiling, which has now elapsed. The operative rights trap for creators is the 2004 digital restoration by the Friedrich-Wilhelm-Murnau-Stiftung, which is the primary version in commercial circulation â€” released by Kino Lorber on Blu-ray with a Neil Brand score and on DVD with a Donald Sosin score, and by Eureka Video (Masters of Cinema) in the UK. That restoration is a separately copyrightable compilation, and each commissioned score is an independently protected composition and sound recording. The 1928 imagery is free; a print sourced from these commercial editions bundles protected elements that travel with any footage extracted from it.
faq: The Kino Lorber Blu-ray says 'Restored Authorized Edition' â€” can I use footage from it?

No, not without a license. The 2004 Murnau Stiftung digital restoration is a separately copyrightable compilation work, and the Neil Brand score on the Blu-ray is an independently copyrighted composition and sound recording. The underlying 1928 film imagery is in the public domain, but those protected elements are embedded in the restoration print and travel with any footage you extract from it. Source a pre-restoration print or verify the provenance of any other copy before relying on it.
Thea von Harbou co-wrote the screenplay â€” does her estate control the underlying story?

No. Von Harbou and Fritz Lang wrote the screenplay as an original work in 1928 for the film itself; her novel of the same title appeared in 1929 only after the film was already in release, so the film was not adapted from a prior published work. As an original 1928 work, the screenplay's US copyright expired January 1, 2024, and no estate claim survives on the story layer.
